what we built: a ruler from worst to best

Three outcomes: a smartphone S (the best), headphones H, a coffee C (the worst).
The best gets utility 1, the worst gets 0.
Every other outcome sits on the ruler at the chance p that makes you indifferent.
H ∼ (S 60%, C 40%), so u(H) = 0.6.
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed).

every lottery on the same ruler

Replace every in-between outcome by its lottery ticket on the best and the worst.
Then every lottery is a chance of the best outcome: that chance is its expected utility.
Lottery 1 (H 40%, C 60%): 0.24. Lottery 2 (S 20%, C 80%): 0.20. Lottery 3 (S 20%, H 30%, C 50%): 0.38.
From now on we only say “best” and “worst”.
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed).

the vNM conditions

If the four conditions below hold, then there exists a utility function u such that you strictly prefer lottery A to lottery B exactly when EU(A) > EU(B).
1 · completeness
2 · transitivity
3 · continuity
4 · independence
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed).

completeness

Assume a good X that you value like (best 60%, worst 40%).
For any two lotteries: you strictly prefer one of them, or you are indifferent.
Every pair of lotteries has an answer.
A violation: one pair has no answer.
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed). Lottery 1 is X for sure, so it is worth 0.6: 1 ≻ 2 (0.6 > 0.5), 3 ≻ 1 (0.7 > 0.6), 3 ≻ 2. The violation is "I can't say, and I am not indifferent either."

transitivity

If lottery 1 is at least as good as lottery 2, and lottery 2 at least as good as lottery 3, then lottery 1 is at least as good as lottery 3.
A violation looks like this: each step seems reasonable, and the last arrow closes a circle.
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed). 1 ≻ 2 and 2 ≻ 3: "almost the same chance, so the larger prize". 3 ≻ 1: "50% against 40% is a real difference, so the safer one". With expected utility, EU(1) > EU(2) > EU(3) > EU(1) is impossible.

continuity

Assume a good X that you value like (best 60%, worst 40%).
continuity
If best ≻ X ≻ worst, then there exists a p between 0 and 1 such that X ∼ (best p, worst 1 − p).
In words: every outcome between the worst and the best is exactly as good as some lottery ticket on the best and the worst.
X ∼ (best 60%, worst 40%): X sits 60% of the way from the worst to the best.
The two numbers are just the chances p and 1 − p. (A mix like this is called a convex combination.)
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed).

continuity: when it fails

Assume a good X that you value like (best 60%, worst 40%).
Raise p, the chance of the best outcome on the lottery ticket.
Continuity: the lottery ticket gets better step by step and crosses X at p = 60%.
A violation: it stays below X for every p below 100% and is better only at 100%: no p makes you indifferent.
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed). "Good" on the vertical axis means only "how much you like it"; no numbers are needed. The right panel is someone for whom any chance of the worst outcome is unacceptable.

independence

Assume a good X that you value like (best 60%, worst 40%).
Adding the same thing to both lotteries, or changing that same thing, must not change your choice.
Step 1: A = X for sure, B = (best 50%, worst 50%). You choose A.
Step 2: with 50% you get your choice, with 50% the worst, in both. Still A.
Step 3: the common half is now the best instead of the worst. Still A.
People do violate this: the Allais paradox, in your problem set.
Wieland 22_choice-theory/frozen/0b33bff24d7d (Ulutin and Gozde passed). EU: step 1 0.6 > 0.5; step 2 0.3 > 0.25; step 3 0.8 > 0.75. The common half adds the same amount to both. Say "independence" only; Arrow's IIA comes later.

utility functions and risk preferences

Remember utility functions over goods, and their indifference curves.
Different functional forms represented different preferences over goods.
The same holds here: utility functions with different shapes represent different preferences over lotteries.
We call these preferences our risk preferences.
Can, Additions 53, 56: goods' graphs, then the same for lotteries; no 'next'.

utility of money

So far the outcomes were things: a smartphone, headphones, a coffee.
Now we think simply in terms of money, with which we can buy things.
Let M be our wealth, in euros.
On the horizontal axis: money M. On the vertical axis: the utility we get from that money, U(M).
We look at three types of curves, one at a time.
Can, Addition 45.

a linear utility function

Equal steps in wealth add equal steps in utility.
Constant marginal utility: each extra euro adds the same.
linear
A function is linear if its graph is a straight line.
An example: U(M) = M.
Can, Additions 45, 48, 56 and 26.11 (steps first, then the line, never both at full strength): the curve, the steps, the card, then the definition with the straight line (steps fade), the formula last.

decreasing marginal utility: a concave function

Equal steps in wealth add less and less utility.
Decreasing marginal utility: each extra euro adds less than the one before.
concave
A function is concave if the straight line between any two points of its graph lies below the graph (or on it).
An example: U(M) = √M.
Can, Additions 45, 48, 56 and 26.11 (steps first, then the line, never both at full strength): the curve, the steps, the card, then the definition with the straight line (steps fade), the formula last.

increasing marginal utility: a convex function

Equal steps in wealth add more and more utility.
Increasing marginal utility: each extra euro adds more than the one before.
convex
A function is convex if the straight line between any two points of its graph lies above the graph (or on it).
An example: U(M) = M².
Can, Additions 45, 48, 56 and 26.11 (steps first, then the line, never both at full strength): the curve, the steps, the card, then the definition with the straight line (steps fade), the formula last.

from utility shapes to risk preferences

We have three shapes of utility: linear, concave and convex.
How do they represent different risk preferences?
And how do we measure a person’s risk preference?
For that we need two concepts: the certainty equivalent and the risk premium.
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): bridge, our lottery ticket, CE, risk premium, the three definitions, then averse, seeking, neutral.

our lottery ticket

A lottery ticket: it pays €6,400 with chance 25% and €0 with chance 75%. You have no other wealth.
Its expected value: EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = €1,600.
Expected utility: multiply the utility of each outcome by its chance, and add up.
In symbols: EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0).
With a linear utility U(M) = M: EU = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600, the same as the expected value: EU = EV.
the lottery ticket
€6,400 with chance 25%
€0 with chance 75%
Can, Addition 56: remind the lottery, the formula step by step, compare with EV. Celebi 26.11 (Can: "example of risk neutral and risk seeking individuals as well and their ce calculations"); numbers passed by Ulutin.

the certainty equivalent

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
certainty equivalent (CE)
The sure amount of money that is exactly as good for you as the lottery ticket.
We find it from U(CE) = EU.
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): bridge, our lottery ticket, CE, risk premium, the three definitions, then averse, seeking, neutral.

the risk premium

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
risk premium
Risk premium = expected value − certainty equivalent.
It is not a payment. It is a gap between two numbers.
On average the lottery ticket pays €1,600 (its expected value). To a risk-averse person (U(M) = √M, coming up next) it is worth only €400 for sure (its certainty equivalent).
The gap, €1,200, is what the risk costs this person: how much less the risky lottery ticket is worth to them than its average payout.
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): bridge, our lottery ticket, CE, risk premium, the three definitions, then averse, seeking, neutral.

risk averse, risk neutral, risk seeking: the definitions

Risk averse: for every risky lottery ticket, your certainty equivalent is below its expected value (risk premium positive).
Risk neutral: always equal (risk premium zero).
Risk seeking: always above (risk premium negative).
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): bridge, our lottery ticket, CE, risk premium, the three definitions, then averse, seeking, neutral. Ulutin: a definition holds for every risky lottery ticket; no strip here.

a risk-averse person: the expected utility

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
U(M) = √M
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
= ¼ · √6,400 + ¾ · √0
= ¼ · 80 + ¾ · 0 = 20
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): step by step, equations on their own lines, the chart in layers.

a risk-averse person: the utility of the expected value

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
First the expected value: EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600.
Its utility, if you had it for sure: U(1,600) = √1,600 = 40.
Why compute it? To compare the lottery ticket with its expected value for sure.
40 > 20: this person prefers €1,600 for sure to the lottery ticket.
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): step by step, equations on their own lines, the chart in layers.

a risk-averse person: finding the certainty equivalent

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
We look for the sure amount CE that is exactly as good as the lottery ticket: U(CE) = EU.
√CE = 20
CE = 20² = 400
€400 for sure is exactly as good as the lottery ticket.
So €400 is what the lottery ticket is worth to this person: they would sell it for any price above €400.
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600
U(CE) = EU
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): step by step, equations on their own lines, the chart in layers.

a risk-averse person: the risk premium

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
risk premium = EV − CE
= 1,600 − 400 = €1,200
The risk makes the lottery ticket worth €1,200 less to this person than its expected value.
Whoever buys it from them for €400 gets €1,600 on average, €1,200 more than they paid: a reward for carrying the risk. That is why it is called a premium.
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600
U(CE) = EU
risk premium = EV − CE
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): step by step, equations on their own lines, the chart in layers.

a risk-seeking person: the expected utility and the utility of the expected value

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
U(M) = M²
EU = ¼ · 6,400² + ¾ · 0² = 10,240,000
U(EV) = 1,600² = 2,560,000
2,560,000 < 10,240,000: this person prefers the lottery ticket to €1,600 for sure.
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600
U(CE) = EU
risk premium = EV − CE
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): step by step, equations on their own lines, the chart in layers.

a risk-seeking person: the certainty equivalent and the risk premium

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
CE² = 10,240,000, so CE = 3,200
risk premium = 1,600 − 3,200 = −€1,600
A negative risk premium: this person values the lottery ticket €1,600 above its expected value.
So €3,200 is what the lottery ticket is worth to this person: they would sell it only for a price above €3,200.
EU = ¼ · U(6,400) + ¾ · U(0)
EV = ¼ · 6,400 + ¾ · 0 = 1,600
U(CE) = EU
risk premium = EV − CE

U(M) = M

CE = 1,600

Risk averse: for every risky lottery ticket, U(expected value) > EU. The curve is concave.
Risk neutral: for every risky lottery ticket, U(expected value) = EU. The curve is linear.
Risk seeking: for every risky lottery ticket, U(expected value) < EU. The curve is convex.

what the certainty equivalent means for prices

Our lottery ticket: €6,400 with chance 25%, €0 with chance 75%. Expected value €1,600.
Suppose you own the lottery ticket. The lowest price at which you would sell it is exactly its certainty equivalent.
The risk-averse person: CE = €400. Below €400 they keep the lottery ticket, above €400 they sell, at exactly €400 they are indifferent.
In terms of the risk premium: CE = EV − risk premium = 1,600 − 1,200 = 400. The risk makes the lottery ticket worth €1,200 less to them than its expected value.
The risk-seeking person: CE = €3,200 = 1,600 − (−1,600). They sell only above €3,200, which is €1,600 more than the expected value.
The risk-neutral person: CE = €1,600. They sell at any price above the expected value.
And buying? If the price is small compared with your wealth, the most you would pay is close to your certainty equivalent (exactly equal for a risk-neutral person). Yesterday’s slider, “the most you would pay”, asked roughly for it.
The certainty equivalent is what the lottery ticket is worth to you, in sure money.
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): 'what does it mean in terms of my willingness to pay'. Ulutin checks; buying and selling prices can differ a little when wealth changes.

CRRA: constant relative risk aversion

Two families of utility functions that economists use a lot, mostly for risk-averse people.
U(M) = M1−r1 − r  for r ≠ 1
U(M) = ln M  for r = 1
M is your wealth, in euros. U(M) is the utility of that wealth.
r is the risk-aversion parameter. r = 0: U(M) = M, risk neutral. The larger r, the more risk averse (r > 0).
Our √M is the case r = ½ (2√M, the same preferences: an affine transformation).
Why “relative”? As you get richer, you put the same share of your wealth into a given risky investment.
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): equations large, what the letters mean, why the names; Arif + Ulutin check. Relative risk aversion r = −M·U''(M)/U'(M) (notes only). Arif (Wikipedia 'Risk aversion'). Example if asked: √M, 50–50 of 16 and 64 has risk premium 4; times 4 (64 or 256) gives 16.

CARA: constant absolute risk aversion

U(M) = 1 − e−aM  with a > 0
e to the power of minus a times M
M is your wealth, in euros. U(M) is the utility of that wealth.
a is the risk-aversion parameter. The larger a, the more risk averse: the curve bends faster.
Why “absolute”? As you get richer, you put the same euro amount into a given risky investment.
Can 26.11 (via Celebi): equations large, what the letters mean, why the names; Arif + Ulutin check. Absolute risk aversion a = −U''(M)/U'(M) (notes only). CARA: add the same amount to every outcome and the risk premium stays the same.

measuring risk preferences

So far we assumed a utility function. But how do we find out a real person’s risk preference?
Economists let people make simple choices with real money and read the risk preference from the choice (here in class without real money).
Three well-known tasks: the bomb box (BRET), the ten choices (Holt and Laury), and asking directly for the certainty equivalent.
Can 26.11: each game a single in-deck poll slide, results like any other poll (Celebi). Carpenter + Ulutin check.

the bomb box (BRET: bomb risk elicitation task)

The original task has 100 boxes (Crosetto and Filippin, 2013). Here is a small version for class, with 12 boxes.
12 boxes. 11 hold €3 each; one hides a bomb. The bomb is in a random box; each box is equally likely to hold the bomb.
You choose how many boxes to open. If the bomb is among them, you get nothing; otherwise €3 per opened box.
What it measures: every extra box adds €3 but raises the chance of losing everything. How far you go shows your risk preference.
How many boxes do you open?
You cannot open all 12: then the bomb is surely among them.
Can 26.11: each game a single in-deck poll slide, results like any other poll (Celebi). Carpenter + Ulutin check. Expected pot k(12 − k)/4: 4 → €8, 6 → €9, 8 → €8.

ten choices (Holt and Laury): how it works

What it measures: how long you stay with the close-together prizes of A before you switch to the far-apart prizes of B.
There are ten rows. In every row you choose between two lottery tickets: option A and option B.
Option A has a high prize of €40 and a low prize of €32.
Option B has a high prize of €77 and a low prize of €2.
The chance of the high prize is the same for A and for B. It changes from row to row: 10% in row 1, 20% in row 2, … 100% in row 10. The low prize comes with the rest.
Row 3, option A:€40 with chance 30%,€32 with chance 70%.
Row 3, option B:€77 with chance 30%,€2 with chance 70%.
Row 1: the high prize has only a 10% chance. A most likely gives €32; B most likely gives €2.
Row 10: the high prize is certain. A is €40 for sure; B is €77 for sure.
Going down the rows, B catches up with A and overtakes it. The row where you switch from A to B shows your risk preference.
Can 26.11: each game a single in-deck poll slide, results like any other poll (Celebi). Carpenter + Ulutin check. The amounts are Holt and Laury (2002)'s $2.00 / $1.60 and $3.85 / $0.10, multiplied by 20 (table checked in 13_book/sources/holt-laury/HL2002_table1_check.md). Risk neutral: first B in row 5.

the class results are on the projector

today in one slide

Utility function U(M)
How much each amount of money is worth to you. Its shape is your risk preference.
Expected value
The average money the lottery ticket pays.
EV = p₁ · M₁ + p₂ · M₂
Expected utility
The average utility the lottery ticket gives.
EU = p₁ · U(M₁) + p₂ · U(M₂)
Certainty equivalent
The sure amount that is exactly as good as the lottery ticket.
U(CE) = EU
Risk premium
EV − CE: how much less a risky lottery ticket is worth to you than its expected value (negative for a risk seeker).
risk premium = EV − CE
Risk attitudes
Risk averse: concave U, CE < EV.
Risk neutral: linear U, CE = EV.
Risk seeking: convex U, CE > EV.
